text:
The docking clamps let go with a sound Mara Voss had never heard from the inside of a ship before—a deep, hydraulic groan that traveled up through the Venture’s spine and into her seat, into her teeth, like the station itself was reluctant to see her go.

“Venture *Nine of Cups*, you are clear of berth fourteen,” traffic control said, bored as a metronome. “Thrusters at your discretion. Please don’t hit anything.”

“Copy, Brelly Control,” Mara said, and then, because her hands were busy and her mouth was not, “No promises.”

The yoke answered her the way she had spent six weeks in simulators teaching it to: light, almost impudent, the little mining frigate swinging its nose out into the berth’s cold blue light. Mara had flown cargo haulers and, once, disastrously, a borrowed shuttle with a sticky port thruster. She had never flown anything that was hers. The *Nine of Cups* was not hers, strictly—she was leased, financed, mortgaged down to the last bolt and every one of those bolts was a debt with Mara’s name on it—but the registry screen said VOSS, M. in clean white letters, and that was close enough to count.

“Final checks,” she said, and thumbed the internal channel. “Imani, tell me something good about my heat exchanger.”

“It’s a heat exchanger,” Imani Rees said from down in the engineering bay, her voice compressed by the intercom into something flat and slightly aggrieved. “It exchanges heat. It does it within tolerance. If you want good, ask for the capacitor.”

“Give me the capacitor.”

“The capacitor is a *poem*, Mara. I rebuilt the tertiary bank myself, by hand, with a torque wrench and the last of my faith in humanity. You could run three cycles back-to-back and she wouldn’t so much as blink.”

“That’s the good I asked for.” Mara ran her eyes down the board: ore hold empty, hold pressure nominal, lasers cold, drones racked and asleep, shield at full. She touched the ore-hold readout out of superstition. Zero point zero cubic meters. The hold smelled, faintly, of the solvent the cleaning crew had used—something sharp and floral, like a rented locker scrubbed by someone who hated flowers. “Jax. Scanner.”

“Scanner’s singing,” Jax Calder said. “Got a clean sweep, got my calibration files from the station survey office, got a spectrum library that *actually* updated for once. You know what the difference is between me and every other scanner operator in this berth?”

“Don’t say it.”

“They guess. I *know*.”

“I walked into that.”

“You walked into it at speed, Captain.”

She wasn’t a captain. Nobody on the squad was anything yet; they had a charter, a shared debt, and a fleet of eight Ventures that the Brelly Station credit union had agreed to finance on the strength of a business plan Imani had written in one night and Mara had proofread twice. But Jax said it with such uncomplicated pleasure that Mara let it stand.

The *Nine of Cups* slid clear of the berth and into the station’s shadow, and then out of it, and the light hit the cockpit glass like a slap. Brelly Station turned slowly behind her, all scaffold and antenna and the long scorched streak where a hauler had once come in hot and left its apology in the plating. Ahead, the other Ventures were shaking loose from their berths one by one: eight small bright hulls, ugly in the way that purpose-built things are ugly, each one carrying an empty hold and a pilot with something to prove.

“*Chorus of Salt*, clear,” said Pell, who flew two berths over and had a habit of narrating her own competence. “*Chorus of Salt*, holding formation point. *Chorus of Salt*, looking extremely good on your scopes.”

“We see you, Pell,” Imani said. “We’re all very impressed.”

“You should be. I waxed my hull.”

“You waxed your *hull*.”

“For luck. And aerodynamics.”

“There’s no air,” Jax said.

“Not with that attitude.”

Okonjo’s *Second Mortgage* came off the clamp last, wobbling slightly, then steadying as Okonjo found his trim. Eight ships. Mara counted them on the scope, then counted them again with her eyes through the glass because she had learned that scopes lied politely and eyes lied honestly.

“Formation, check in,” she said, and heard them come back in ragged order: Pell, Okonjo, Hess, the *Damp Squib*, the *Ore Nothing*, the twins in *Two Buckets*, the *Long Odds*, and Jax in her ear saying, “*Nine of Cups*, sweet and clear.”

“All present,” Mara said. “Brelly Control, fleet of eight Ventures, departing for B-7. Filing transit now.”

“B-7 acknowledged,” Control said. “Be advised, belt traffic is light, claim board is open, and the last squad out there made fourteen thousand credits in a week and then lost a drone to a rock that they swear moved.”

“Rocks don’t move,” Imani said.

“That’s what they said.”

Mara pushed the throttle up in increments, feeling the push settle into her back, and the station fell away behind them in a slow tumble of light. “Course laid in,” she said. “B-7, two hours twenty. Comms quiet after the burn, keep your eyes on your own boards. And Pell—”

“Yes, Mara.”

“Stop waxing things.”

The burn was long and boring, which was the best thing a burn could be. Jax read rock spectra out loud until Imani threatened to mute him. Imani told a story about a coolant line that had failed on a station she’d worked and the man who had fixed it with chewing gum—a lie, Mara was fairly sure, but a good one. Mara ate a ration bar that tasted of cardboard and ambition and watched the scanner paint the outer system in patient green arcs. Sunlight. Dust. Nothing that wanted to kill them yet.

B-7 arrived as a smear, and then as specks, and then as a belt: a slow gray river of stone tumbling in the dark, some of it no bigger than a fist, some of it large enough to have a name. The claim beacons blinked along the belt’s near edge, unclaimed slots and claimed ones, and the marked slots were few.

“Claim board,” Jax said, all the joke gone out of his voice. “Slot fourteen-C through twenty-two-C, transferring to squad registry. Confirming.”

Mara brought the fleet in on the near edge, brakes feathering, and the *Nine of Cups* came to rest relative to a rock the size of a warehouse with a nineteen percent yield reading and a bad attitude. One by one the others matched her, eight ships hanging in the dust with their lasers cold and their holds empty.

“Registered,” Jax said. “We hold claim.”

“Say it properly,” Imani said.

“We hold claim,” Jax said, and then, because he couldn’t help it, “and for the record, I called the primary before any of you had your boots on.”

Mara keyed the mining channel. “Squad, this is Voss. Claim is ours, belt is ours, ore is theoretically ours. Lasers hot in ten. Let’s find out what we’re worth.”

The beacons blinked green across the board, and eight empty holds turned toward the rock.

text:
Jax Calder had been telling people for six weeks that a scanner was not a metal detector and that the difference mattered, and now, with the B-7 belt turning slow and gray outside the *Nine of Cups*'s glass, he finally had an audience that couldn't walk away.

"See, a metal detector says *something's there*," he said, sweeping the primary's return across three screens. "A scanner says *what*, and *how much*, and *where it's hiding*. That rock right there —" he tapped the display, and the tap made the whole spectral stack shiver "— is nineteen percent by mass, mostly nickel-iron with a nickel silicate rind, and there's a seam in her like a good vein in a bad tooth."

"How do you know it's a seam?" Mara said, not looking up from her trim.

"Because I know things."

"He guesses," Imani said, from the bay.

"I *know*." He pulled the return into close focus, dumped it through the calibration files he'd argued with the survey office about for two days, and waited for the model to finish telling him what he'd already told himself. The rock's limb smeared into a bright banded line. Around the seventh pass, the banding knuckled, bunched, and went hot. "There. Look at that. That's not rind, that's a lode. High-grade, shallow, maybe forty meters in from the sunward face. We could cut that with a butter knife."

"You don't have a butter knife," Imani said.

"I have a very expensive laser."

"Whose lease payment is due on the ninth," Mara said.

"It's the sixth."

"Then we have three days to be brilliant."

Jax leaned back. The chair in the *Nine of Cups* had been broken when they bought her and he had personally fixed the recline with a cable tie and optimism, and it held, and he let it hold. This was the part he'd promised himself. Not the undocking, not the burn — the moment when a rock stopped being a number and started being ore. "Fleet channel," he said. "Everyone listen. I'm sending the seam map now. Cut on my marks and you'll all be rich by dinner. Well. Rich adjacent."

"You've been wrong before," Okonjo said, from the *Second Mortgage*.

"I've been *early* before. There's a difference."

"The last time you were early, we spent nine hours boring a hole in a rock that turned out to be a rock."

"That rock had potential."

"It had *nothing*, Jax."

"It had potential."

They cut on his marks anyway — that was the thing about being the scanner on a squad of rookies, everyone wanted to be the one who'd believed. Eight Ventures spread along the sunward face in a loose comb, lasers cold, drones racked. Pell's *Chorus of Salt* took the high edge and, for reasons of her own, announced it.

"*Chorus of Salt* on station. Sunward face. It's beautiful out here, you know? Very —" a pause "— rock-forward."

"Pell," Mara said, "save the poetry for the broadcast."

Imani went out on tether to set the charges. Jax watched her go on the externals, a small bright shape drifting out from the *Nine of Cups*'s flank with a toolbag the size of a coffin, and he thought about how the only thing between Imani Rees and a very long fall was a line rated for four hundred kilos and her own opinion of herself.

"Charges set," Imani said, forty minutes later. "Low-yield, shaped, three in a row along the seam. When these go, the face comes off like a scab. Nobody be in front of it."

"Nobody's in front of it," said Hess.

"Somebody's always in front of it."

The charges went. The rock did what rock does under shaped charges, which is to say it came apart with enormous dignity and no drama at all, slow in vacuum, a wall of stone peeling off and tumbling away in a beautiful gray curve, and behind it: the lode, bright and clean as a struck bell, the exposed face throwing back the fleet's work lights in fat metallic gleams.

Jax whooped. He was not ashamed of it.

"*There* it is," he said. "Ladies and gentlemen, the seam. Look at her. She's gorgeous. She's the most beautiful thing I've ever seen and I've seen Pell's hull."

"Everyone's seen Pell's hull," Imani said. "She waxed it."

The drone work began in quiet chaos. The *Nine of Cups* put out two of her four harvesters, and one of them — Jax would later insist this was a calibration issue and not, as Imani put it, a piloting issue — came in at the wrong angle and bounced off the seam face, tumbling, righting itself with an aggrieved chirp, then banging the rock again.

"Jax."

"That's not me."

"Your drone."

"It's a *shared* drone."

"Bring it home before it breaks its nose." Imani's voice had the flat patience of a woman who could hear the impact in the hull. "Come left, come left, no — your other left. Good. Now *slow*. Slow. Slow. There."

It came back with its scoop half full and its shell scratched to ruin, and Jax loved it, and the hold began, increment by increment, to fill: the ore readout climbing off zero point zero for the first time in the *Nine of Cups*'s mortgaged life. He watched the number like a man watching his firstborn learn to walk and he narrated every increment, and by the fourth ton Pell had started calling him "the accountant" and Okonjo had stopped complaining about the rock with potential.

"Nineteen percent," Jax said. "Fourteen tons cut and my numbers haven't moved. Told you. Told all of you."

"You told us," Mara said, and then, gently: "Keep it on the internal, Jax. Every other squad in the belt doesn't need to hear you gloat."

He laughed, said "No promises," and forgot about it in nine seconds.

That was the trouble, though he wouldn't know it for another hour. The mining channel stayed hot the whole shift, because they were rookies and rookies talk: Pell narrating her cuts, the twins in *Two Buckets* arguing about whose turn it was to log the tonnage, Okonjo's honest delight each time his hold gained a percent, Imani yelling up the intercom that somebody's tertiary capacitor was drawing dirty and somebody was going to answer to her personally. And beneath the chatter, under everything, the *Nine of Cups* was also broadcasting something she couldn't help: the deep warm thrum of an operating plant, four lasers jackhammering a seam, heat dumping to radiator, drone telemetry whining out in all directions like a dinner bell rung by a very enthusiastic hand.

Jax saw the contact at 1841 and didn't think much of it.

"Hey," he said, "got a hull on the long sweep. Outer edge, past the claim beacons. Six — no, seven hundred klicks."

Mara leaned over. "Miner?"

"Return's too tight for a Venture. Not a hauler either." He ran the profile. "Could be a prospector. Could be a survey drone tender." The spectrum resolved one more notch and he frowned at it without understanding what he was frowning at, because the signature was small and fast and sitting perfectly still, the way a thing sits still when it is watching rather than drifting. Then the return smeared, and a rock went through the beam, and when it cleared there was nothing on the sweep but stone.

"Lost it," he said.

"Log it," Mara said. "We'll report it at the shift change."

"Probably nothing."

"Probably," she said, and turned back to her trim, and the lasers kept hammering, and Jax went back to his beautiful seam, and eight empty-ish holds turned their work lights on the rock and talked, cheerfully and unencrypted, into the dark.

Mara felt the ore hold pass sixteen tons and allowed herself exactly four seconds of satisfaction. On the *Nine of Cups*’s main display, the lode shone like a fresh wound in the rock, bright and orderly, and the fleet’s eight work lights made a little constellation around it.

“Sixteen point two,” Jax said. “Sixteen point three. She’s still nineteen percent, Mara. She’s still —”

“I heard you the first fifty times.”

“I’m narrating for posterity.”

“Posterity’s trying to fly.”

Pell was singing something off-key on the mining channel. Okonjo was arguing with one of the twins about tonnage logs. Imani had come up from the bay long enough to stand behind Mara’s seat with a mug of station coffee and the expression of a woman listening to her own engines for signs of betrayal.

Then Jax stopped narrating.

“Contact,” he said. “Same bearing. Six hundred klicks. No — three contacts. Four.”

Mara looked. The returns came in clean and fast, no longer trying to hide. One was broad and heavy, its profile like a hammerhead shark made of welded armor. The other was slim, needle-nosed, burning hot.

“Marmite,” Jax said, and his voice had gone very quiet. “That’s a Cyclone. And a Stiletto running her screen.”

The mining channel went silent in a way that had nothing to do with discipline. Everyone had heard the name. The Marmite Collective did not prospect. They did not negotiate. They arrived, they cut your drives, they took your holds, and if you were lucky they left you a beacon to call for rescue.

“All ships,” Mara said. “Cold lasers. Rack drones. Dump the mining channel. Now.”

A new voice came over the emergency band, smooth as a sales pitch. “B-7 independents, this is the Marmite Collective. You are operating in a protected transit corridor. Your vessels and cargo are now subject to salvage assessment. Cut thrust, kill your reactors, and prepare to receive boarding parties. Resistance will be considered a waiver of your insurance.”

“Protected transit corridor,” Imani said. “That’s new.”

“Mara,” Okonjo said. “They’re launching.”

The Cyclone’s bays opened. Four raider cutters spat out and came in on divergent vectors, while the Stiletto surged ahead, its engines a hard blue line. The pirate frigate held back, patient as a creditor.

The Stiletto fired first.

It was not a missile. It was a rail round, and Mara did not see it so much as feel the *Nine of Cups* flinch as it passed close enough to rattle her teeth. Then the raiders opened up, and the dark between the rocks filled with brief white lines.

“Go, go, go!”

The fleet came apart. Eight Ventures were not a formation anymore; they were eight panicked bright shapes diving into a gray river of stone. “Jax, give me a route!”

“I’m giving you a route!”

“Give me a *better* one!”

“There’s a Coriolis mess at two o’clock, then a clear lane behind the big iron — wait. Wait. Hess is hit.”

“Hess!” Mara keyed the channel. “Hess, answer.”

Mara had one clear thought, and it was not a good one, and she did it anyway. “Okonjo, Pell, cover me. I’m going back.”

“Mara —” Imani started.

“I’m going back.”

She reversed thrust so hard the harness cut into her shoulders. The *Nine of Cups* swung around a rock the size of a cathedral and came at the *Damp Squib* from its blind side, braking and matching tumble with short, brutal bursts. Jax called the closure rates like a man reading a prayer. Okonjo’s *Second Mortgage* cut across the Stiletto’s nose, lasers still cold, but the pirate had to veer or risk the rocks. Pell’s *Chorus of Salt* dumped a rack of empty ore canisters into the lane behind them, and the Stiletto’s pilot, suddenly presented with a hundred tumbling sensor ghosts, chose caution.

“Grapnel,” Mara said. “Imani, give me the magnetic grapnel.”

“It’s rated for one point five Ventures.”

“Hess’s ship is half a Venture now. Do it.”

The *Nine of Cups* shuddered as the grapnel caught. The *Damp Squib* jerked, straightened, and then came with them, a dead weight on a line, sparks spitting from her ruined drive.

“Fleet, follow me,” Mara said. “Through the field. We’re going dark.”

“Brelly Station is the other way,” one of the twins said.

“Brelly Station has a Cyclone sitting on its approach. Follow me.”

Jax found them a corridor. He did it with his voice pitched low and fast, calling rocks and rotations and clearances, and Mara flew it with the grapnel dragging behind her like an anchor and the Stiletto somewhere in the dust, hunting. When the pirate frigate finally came into the field, it came slowly, the way a big animal enters a thicket, and by then the eight Ventures — seven under power, one in tow — had threaded into a dark seam of the belt where the rock was old and depleted and the returns were dirty.

“Ice,” Jax said. “Big pocket. Depleted, no volatiles worth claiming, and the surface is rough enough to scatter us. It’s a hole in the scanner.”

“In,” Mara said.

They went in one by one, work lights off, reactors throttled to a whisper. The ice pocket was a hollow tumor in the belt’s oldest rock, rimmed with frost and black dust. The *Nine of Cups* drifted to a stop with the *Damp Squib* tethered behind her, and the last of the fleet tucked itself into the shadows of the cave’s mouth.

For a long moment nobody spoke.

Then Imani said, from the engineering bay, “Reactor’s hot. Coolant’s marginal. My tertiary capacitor is doing that thing again.”

“What thing?” Mara said.

“The thing where it’s a poem.”

Mara laughed. It came out cracked and strange. The tactical plot showed no immediate pursuit, but the Marmite signatures were still there, a Cyclone and a Stiletto and their cutters, sweeping the belt between the ice pocket and Brelly Station.

“They’re not leaving,” Jax said.

“No,” Mara said. “They’re waiting.”

Hess’s voice came over the channel, tinny and exhausted. “Mara. I’ve got three injured. Nothing critical. I’ve got no drive, no main bus, and my hull is open to vacuum in two compartments.”

“We’ll patch you.”

“With what?”

“With whatever Imani finds.”

Imani appeared in the cockpit doorway, wiping her hands on a rag. “I can give you a patched bus. I can give you a drive if we cannibalize the *Long Odds*’ spare coils. But I can’t get us past a Cyclone with cold lasers and seven limping boats.”

Mara looked at the plot. Then at the ice around them, thick and silent and full of nothing the pirates wanted. Then at the eight little icons of her fleet.

“Maybe not cold,” she said.

Jax turned in his chair. “Mara.”

“Not yet.” She put her hand on the yoke, not to move it, just to feel it there. “First we make sure everyone’s alive. Then we make sure everyone’s angry. Then we see what a squad of rookies with mining lasers can do to a Cyclone that thinks it’s already won.”

text:
The ice pocket had a sound, and Jax hated it.

Not a real sound—nothing out here carried, and the rock was too old and too cold to tick. It was the hull itself, the *Nine of Cups* talking to herself in tiny thermal moans as the last of her heat bled into the frost, a ship cooling off in a hole in the dark. Every twenty minutes or so, a fleck of dust would ping off the plating and Jax would flinch.

“You’re doing it again,” Imani said. She was up in the cockpit now, wedged into the jump seat with her boots braced against the console frame and a coil of spare line across her knees, splicing something by feel in the dark.

“Doing what?”

“Whispering ‘huh’ at your scanner like it’s going to answer.”

“It might.” He tapped the passive array, coaxed the gain up another notch, and the display bloomed with a slow gray snowfall that was the B-7 belt seen through a cave mouth. “Nobody’s pinged. Nobody’s sweeping. Nine hours and the only thing that’s moved out there is rock.” He said the last word like it was a personal insult.

“And Hess?”

“Hess has a bus limping and two compartments full of vacuum and she’s still carving deck plating off the *Long Odds* for a patch. She’s fine. She’s the finest woman in the belt, actually, according to her.”

Imani snorted. Then she said, quietly, “Passive only. We agreed.”

“I know what we agreed.”

The fleet sat in the cave mouth with its eyes shut. It was the strangest thing Jax had ever been part of—eight ships, sixty-odd people, one very expensive silence—and the discipline of it was starting to fray at the edges in ways that showed up as small, unnecessary transmissions. Pell had asked twice whether anyone else’s recycling smelled like a wet dog. One of the twins had requested a ruling on whether the ice counted as claimable. Mara had answered both with a single word each, delivered with the flat finality of a door closing.

At 0312 by the *Nine of Cups*’s stubborn old chrono, passive gave Jax a drive flare.

“Contact,” he said, and Mara was awake in her seat before he’d finished the word, which meant she’d never been asleep. “Station side. Inbound fast, one hull—that’s a big torch for a single hull.” He pulled the spectrum in, and then he stopped breathing for a second, because the transponder was squawking open and unencrypted in the clear. “Militia.”

“Say again.”

“Brelly Militia cutter, running her colors hot. Stiletto-class, she’s—” He squinted. Read the registry string twice. “She’s the *Reasonable Doubt*.”

“That’s a militia name?” Imani said.

“That’s a *lovely* militia name.”

The *Reasonable Doubt* came in from the station vector at three-quarters throttle, transponder bellowing, and she was broadcasting on every band at once: this is a Brelly Militia vessel, disengage and disperse, you are conducting unlawful salvage in a registered corridor, this is your only warning, and so on down to the point where the voice on the recording sounded like it had said the words so many times that the meaning had worn off them.

The Cyclone did not scatter. It turned, unhurried, like a man putting down his cup to deal with a rude guest.

“She’s alone,” Jax said. “There’s no second hull behind her. There’s no—” He widened the sweep, hunted the edges, found nothing but belt. “Mara. There’s no second hull.”

“They sent one cutter,” Mara said.

The Cyclone answered the hail on the open band, in that same oiled voice from before, and Jax heard the moment it stopped being a sales pitch.

“Brelly Militia, this is the *Marrow*. You are pursuing a civil salvage claim between private parties. Stand down or be assessed.”

The militia pilot—young, Jax thought; young in a way she was working hard to bury under procedure—said, “You are not a private party, you are the *Marmite Collective*, and you are going to release those vessels and come about and follow me back to station, or I’m going to put a round through your number three bay.”

Then she did it.

The *Reasonable Doubt* opened up—spinal rail into the Cyclone's flank, point defense into the nearest raider cutter. The rail round hit hard enough that the whole passive array chimed. The cutter came apart at the shoulder, venting, spinning out. The Cyclone's shields rippled in a crescent of pale fire.

Jax heard himself laughing. “She got him. She *got* him—”

“Jax,” Imani said.

The Cyclone turned into her, deliberately, the way a wrestler gives ground he doesn't need. The torches of the cutters swung in behind the militia cutter, and the Marmite Stiletto came up out of the belt's shadow—not out of nowhere, Jax would tell himself later. The big iron rock at ten o'clock threw a thermal halo that swallowed anything small and cold, and the Stiletto had spent hours in its lee with her reactor damped to a whisper and her transponder dark, her return eaten by the same rough stone that was hiding the fleet. Passive had read her as rock because she had made herself into rock. He had looked. He had looked at the wrong shadow.

The cutters came in first—three of them on a curve that would have been pretty if it hadn't been aimed at a militia hull. The *Reasonable Doubt* turned into them instead of away, her point defense opening in short, barking bursts. One cutter took a hit and peeled off trailing atmosphere. But the Stiletto was working around the outside of the fight, patient and blue, taking her time, and the Cyclone kept coming, unhurried, its bays cycling behind the damage it had already soaked up. Jax watched the militia cutter weave through it, taking hits she couldn't afford, and understood with a sick drop in his stomach that she wasn't trying to win. She was trying to make enough noise that Brelly Station would hear her die.

The militia cutter put her second round into the Cyclone’s armor and it detonated flat and useless against the plate. Then the Cyclone’s missile bays flushed and the *Reasonable Doubt* disappeared inside a lattice of white, her shields going from bright to gray to gone in three stages, each one marked by a cheer from the Marmite channel that Jax could hear bleeding raw through the ice.

“Shield’s down,” he said, and his voice had gone thin. “She’s lost her main drive. She’s tumbling. Cutters are closing.”

“She’s talking,” Imani said.

She was. The open band had gone to pieces, and through it came the militia pilot’s voice, steady and much younger than procedure, saying: “Brelly Station, Brelly Station, *Reasonable Doubt* declaring an emergency, I am—” a pause, a breath, a sound like metal being torn “—I am weapons dark, drive dark, I am not going to make the station, I have—” and then she stopped, and came back, and said, “There’s nobody else coming. Is there. There’s nobody else coming, is there.”

The Cyclone had stopped firing. It didn’t need to. It was drifting in with its cutters spread, taking its time.

In the *Nine of Cups* cockpit, the silence was very exact.

“Seven ships,” Imani said, at last, into it. “Seven limping boats and cold lasers. That’s what we’ve got. If we go out there we don’t save her, we just add eight names to the report.”

“Yes,” Mara said.

“Mara.”

“Imani.” Mara hadn't moved her hand off the yoke—hadn't, Jax realized, moved it since the contact alarm. Her voice was the quietest thing in the cabin, quieter than the hull's cooling moans. “If they take her apart out there, we're a cave. We're four hundred tons of ore in a hole, and they'll come in here methodical, one mouth at a time, and it'll take them an afternoon.” She turned her head, and Jax watched her eyes go around the cockpit—Imani, him, the dark beyond the glass—and something in her face settle like a charge seating itself. “Jax. The *Marrow*'s shield. Where's it thin?”

Jax had the data. He didn’t remember pulling it up; his hands had done it while his mouth was being clever, and now he looked at the geometry and understood exactly what she was asking, and his stomach turned over, and he told her anyway. “Forward quadrant, low. She took the militia’s round there and it bloomed. She’s got a notch in the emitter ring, right about—” he tapped “—there. And she’s got four bays and she just flushed three of them, so she’s reloading.”

“How long?”

“Eight minutes. Maybe nine.”

Mara keyed the fleet channel. Jax had heard her give a lot of orders in six weeks and this was the first one that wasn’t a course correction.

“All ships. This is Voss. We’re going out.” Her thumb stayed down on the key. “Cold lasers aren’t going to do it, so we don’t fight her like a frigate. We fight her like a rock. Nobody moves until I say and then everybody moves at once, and if you are not certain—I mean certain down to your teeth—then you stay in the pocket and nobody will hold it against you, and I’ll see you at the bar.”

The channel hissed. Then:

“*Chorus of Salt*,” Pell said, and for once she didn’t narrate her own competence. “We’re in.”

“*Second Mortgage*, in.”

“*Ore Nothing*, in.”

“*Long Odds*—we’re running on half a bus and spite, and we’re in.”

“*Two Buckets*,” said the twins, in ragged unison. Then, from a hull Jax had half forgotten was out there: “*Grace Period*. We're in. We're not even scratched.”

And then, thin, furious, from behind them on the grapnel line: “*Damp Squib*,” Hess said. “I can’t fly. Put me in the front and I’ll be the anvil.”

Mara let out a breath that was almost a laugh. “Nobody’s the anvil,” she said. “Jax. Give me a route out of this hole that doesn’t look like a charge.”

The *Nine of Cups* came alive under Jax’s hands, board by board, her reactor stepping up out of its whisper into a warm and audible roar, her work lights slamming on and turning the frost around them into a blowing white nothing. On the tactical plot the other seven lit up after her, one after another, brightest thing in the belt, and Jax leaned into the scanner and began to call the way out.

She was trying to make enough noise that Brelly Station would hear her die.
The militia cutter put her second round into the Cyclone’s armor and it detonated flat and useless against the plate.

Then the Cyclone’s missile bays flushed and the *Reasonable Doubt* disappeared inside a lattice of white, her shields going from bright to gray to gone in three stages, each one marked by a cheer from the Marmite channel that Jax could hear bleeding raw through the ice.
“Shield’s down,” he said, and his voice had gone thin.
“She’s lost her main drive.
She’s tumbling.
Cutters are closing.”
“She’s talking,” Imani said.
She was.

The open band had gone to pieces, and through it came the militia pilot’s voice, steady and much younger than procedure, saying: “Brelly Station, Brelly Station, *Reasonable Doubt* declaring an emergency, I am—” a pause, a breath, a sound like metal being torn “—I am weapons dark, drive dark, I am not going to make the station, I have—” and then she stopped, and came back, and said, “There’s nobody else coming.
Is there.
There’s nobody else coming, is there.”
The Cyclone had stopped firing.
It didn’t need to.
It was drifting in with its cutters spread, taking its time.
In the *Nine of Cups* cockpit, the silence was very exact.
“Seven ships,” Imani said, at last, into it.
“Seven limping boats and cold lasers.
That’s what we’ve got.
If we go out there we don’t save her, we just add eight names to the report.”
“Yes,” Mara said.
“Mara.”
“Imani.”
Mara hadn't moved her hand off the yoke—hadn't, Jax realized, moved it since the contact alarm.
Her voice was the quietest thing in the cabin, quieter than the hull's cooling moans.
“If they take her apart out there, we're a cave.
We're four hundred tons of ore in a hole, and they'll come in here methodical, one mouth at a time, and it'll take them an afternoon.”
She turned her head, and Jax watched her eyes go around the cockpit—Imani, him, the dark beyond the glass—and something in her face settle like a charge seating itself.
“Jax.
The *Marrow*'s shield.
Where's it thin?”
Jax had the data.

He didn’t remember pulling it up; his hands had done it while his mouth was being clever, and now he looked at the geometry and understood exactly what she was asking, and his stomach turned over, and he told her anyway.
“Forward quadrant, low.
She took the militia’s round there and it bloomed.
She’s got a notch in the emitter ring, right about—” he tapped “—there.
And she’s got four bays and she just flushed three of them, so she’s reloading.”
“How long?”
“Eight minutes.
Maybe nine.”
Mara keyed the fleet channel.
Jax had heard her give a lot of orders in six weeks and this was the first one that wasn’t a course correction.
“All ships.
This is Voss.
We’re going out.”
Her thumb stayed down on the key.
“Cold lasers aren’t going to do it, so we don’t fight her like a frigate.
We fight her like a rock.

Nobody moves until I say and then everybody moves at once, and if you are not certain—I mean certain down to your teeth—then you stay in the pocket and nobody will hold it against you, and I’ll see you at the bar.”
The channel hissed.
Then:
“*Chorus of Salt*,” Pell said, and for once she didn’t narrate her own competence.
“We’re in.”
“*Second Mortgage*, in.”
“*Ore Nothing*, in.”
“*Long Odds*—we’re running on half a bus and spite, and we’re in.”
“*Two Buckets*,” said the twins, in ragged unison.
Then, from a hull Jax had half forgotten was out there: “*Grace Period*.
We're in.
We're not even scratched.”
And then, thin, furious, from behind them on the grapnel line: “*Damp Squib*,” Hess said.
“I can’t fly.
Put me in the front and I’ll be the anvil.”
Mara let out a breath that was almost a laugh.
“Nobody’s the anvil,” she said.
“Jax.
Give me a route out of this hole that doesn’t look like a charge.”

The *Nine of Cups* came alive under Jax’s hands, board by board, her reactor stepping up out of its whisper into a warm and audible roar, her work lights slamming on and turning the frost around them into a blowing white nothing.
On the tactical plot the other seven lit up after her, one after another, brightest thing in the belt, and Jax leaned into the scanner and began to call the way out.

text:
Jax had the route out of the pocket laid down in his head—two rocks, a gap, a shadow—and he was halfway through calling it when the belt put something else on his screen.

“Hold,” he said. “Hold, hold, hold.”

“Jax.”

“I know. I’m calling the route and I’m also—” He pulled the return in, pushed it through the model, and the model came back with a shape he didn’t like and couldn’t stop looking at. “Mara, kill the burn.”

“Say why.”

“Because there’s a rock in the lane and I think it’s the reason we win.”

The *Nine of Cups*’s reactor settled back a notch. Out past the glass, the belt turned its patient gray, and somewhere in it the Cyclone *Marrow* was closing on a tumbling militia cutter with its bays cycling and its forward shield flickering where the round had bloomed it.

“Talk,” Mara said.

“Her.” Jax threw the rock onto the main display, a lumpy two-hundred-meter potato of nickel-iron with a bad seam down its middle. He ran the deep scan and the return came back wrong in the best way—hollow-sounding, banded, full of bright lines. “She’s not solid. Something hit her once and left a fault plane with a silicate band along it, and stress fractures running out from it like a spider. She’s pre-broken. She’s a stack of dinner plates held together by guilt.”

“And?”

“And if I cut her on the fault, she comes apart in a sheet. Not a cloud. A sheet. A flat wall of junk moving wherever I tell the charges to push it.”

Imani’s voice came from the jump seat, flat and quick. “How flat?”

“Like a shotgun. If we trench her along the plane first, the break follows the trench. We can shape it into a cone.”

Mara was quiet for exactly as long as it took her to look at the plot, at the Cyclone, at the militia cutter dying by inches. “How long does the Cyclone take to reload?”

“Six minutes now,” Jax said. “Maybe five.”

“Imani. How long to make a rock into a shotgun?”

“Charges in the trench, shaped, low-yield, like we did on the lode but bigger. Four minutes if somebody else cuts the trench.”

“Then we cut the trench,” Mara said, and keyed the fleet channel, and her voice went out clean and even and completely without apology. “All ships. New plan. We’re not dying for a militia we don’t know, and we’re not dying in a cave. We’re going to drop a mountain on a frigate. Jax has the target; Imani has the charges; if I tell you to cut a line, you cut it and you don’t ask me why until the shooting stops. Hess.”

“Here.”

“You can’t fly and you can’t fight, so you’re going to be the most useful ship in the belt. We’re casting you loose. Hold the pocket mouth on maneuvering thrusters. If anything comes at us from behind, dump your ore in its path and use the rocks it makes.”

A pause, then Hess, dry as a will: “That’s not an anvil. That’s a gutter.”

“It’s a gutter,” Mara agreed. “Welcome to the plan.”

They went out of the pocket in a line and turned broadside to the belt, and for ninety seconds the fleet did the only thing it had ever been built to do. Pell took the high face; Okonjo took the low. The *Ore Nothing* and the twins in *Two Buckets* came in along the fault line with their strip miners burning in long mode, and the rock answered with a shriek of vaporized silicate that Jax heard through the hull as a hum in his teeth. Four lasers. Four trenches, shallow, converging, cut along his marks.

“Left ship’s drifting,” he said. “Pell, you’re two meters off the plane.”

“I am *not*.”

“You are *entirely*.”

“I’m correcting.” A pause. “Corrected. And for the record, that rock is hideous. It looks like a potato that lost an argument.”

“It’s the most beautiful thing I’ve ever seen,” Jax said, “and I’ve seen your hull.”

“You’re both very funny,” Imani said, going out the lock with a toolbag and a line. “Nobody be in front of it.”

“Somebody’s always—” Pell started.

“Don’t.”

Imani went out on the tether and set the charges in the trenches by hand while the clock in Jax’s head counted down from four, and the Cyclone grew in the plot—unhurried, deliberate, bringing its nose around toward the militia cutter’s drifting hull.

“She’s going to fire,” Jax said. “Mara, she’s going to fire on the militia.”

“Imani.”

“I’m set.” Her voice was thin with effort. “Charges in. Arming. Give me a ten count and get everybody on the far side of that rock.”

Mara keyed the channel. “Fleet, all ships, break to the far side and turn your glass away from the blast. That’s an order that includes your work lights, Pell.”

“I—”

“*Pell*.”

The lights went out. Seven ships slid around the potato’s shadow in a scatter, and the *Nine of Cups* came around last, reactor stepped up and Mara’s hands full, and Jax watched his screen and saw exactly the wrong thing.

“The Cyclone’s turning,” he said. “She’s coming around. She’s going to miss the cone.”

“Where’s she going?”

“Toward the militia—no. Wait.” He read the geometry, and his heart did something ugly. “She’s coming toward *us*. She’s going to take us before she finishes the cutter. Mara, she’s on the lane.”

“Is the rock still in the lane?”

“Yes.”

“Then so is she,” Mara said. “Imani. Blow it.”

“Ten,” Imani said. “Nine. Eight. You want to be turned away.”

The fleet turned away. Jax did not. He watched the rock with his scanner wide open and his hands flat on the console, because somebody had to call what came next, and it was his name on the sensor log, and he was not going to miss it.

“Four. Three. Two.”

The charges went off along the trench in a ripple, shaped and low, and the potato came apart exactly the way he had promised it would—no drama, no fireball, just the plane giving way and two hundred meters of nickel-iron peeling into a sheet and the sheet breaking into a wedge and the wedge throwing itself outward in a flat gray fan of stone and metal and dust. It was the biggest thing that had ever happened in front of his eyes.

The fan crossed the lane at a closing speed of kilometers per second, because the Cyclone was already driving into it.

The Marmite frigate's point defense opened up and took a third of the shrapnel out of the air, and the rest hit the forward quadrant low, exactly where the militia's rail round had bloomed the emitter ring—a sandblaster on a wound. Jax watched the shield go from clean to cloudy to a lattice of white lines to something like cracked ice, and then the whole forward ring failed in a cascade of pale fire and the shrapnel began to arrive on the armor behind it.

“Shield's down,” he said. “Shield's *down*. She's taking it on the plate. She's—” A bay went up. Not the hull, just a bay, a bright bloom of a reloaded missile deciding it had opinions, and the *Marrow* staggered, and something long and structural came off her flank and turned slowly end over end into the dark. “She's hurt. She's hurt bad. Her starboard bays are gutted.”

The pirate cutters broke first, peeling away in two directions. On the open band someone was shouting, the oiled voice gone ragged, and Jax heard it and laughed out loud, an ugly laugh, and then he looked at the militia cutter and stopped.

“The *Reasonable Doubt*,” he said. “Her bow's coming around. She's got maneuvering. She's got—”

Mara was already on it. “Militia cutter, this is Voss of the B-7 independents. We've opened her up. If you've got a round left, put it in her starboard number three bay.”

A long hiss of a carrier. Then, hoarse and improbably young: “I've got one round left. I've had one round left for ten minutes. I was saving it.”

“Spend it,” Mara said.

The rail round went through the Cyclone's opened flank and detonated inside her. For a moment her number three bay looked like the inside of a furnace, and then the *Marrow* came off her line, her drives stuttering, her hull venting in three long white feathers.

Then the Stiletto came back.

Then the Marmite Stiletto came back.

“She's screening her,” Jax said. “She's covering the frigate while she comes back to herself. Mara, they're not running.”

“No,” Mara said. “They're rallying.”

Imani came back through the lock with her toolbag and her hair standing up and her face the color of bad coffee. “Charges spent. Tether stowed. Somebody tell me the capacitor held.”

“The capacitor held,” Jax said.

“You're lying.”

“It held,” Mara said, and turned the *Nine of Cups*'s nose toward the reforming line of pirates with the work lights coming back up and the fleet behind her in the dark, bright and small and all of it still there.

text:
The office had gone quiet in the way large buildings do when most of their people have left: not silence, but a held breath. Nora sat at her desk on the fourth floor of Reddit HQ with her cardigan sleeves pushed to her elbows and the last of a cold coffee turning into a brown ring inside the mug. Beyond the glass, the city lights were doing their usual expensive imitation of stars. Inside, the fluorescent panels hummed at a pitch that made her teeth feel loose.

She had been running the audit for nine hours.

It was not glamorous work. The deprecated-services log sweep was the kind of task handed to junior engineers because it required patience, credential hygiene, and no imagination whatsoever. Every quarter, some cluster or queue or forgotten cron job got marked for decommissioning, and someone had to prove its logs had been retained correctly, purged correctly, and hadn’t quietly leaked user data into some bucket nobody owned anymore. Nora had written the parser herself. She called it Cinder because it burned through old records and left only the ash of compliance.

Cinder had processed 4.8 million entries since morning. It had found three malformed timestamps, one duplicated request ID, and a service account with a password so old it was practically archaeological. All of it had gone into a tidy report with green checkmarks and a paragraph her manager would not read.

At 8:47 p.m., Cinder found something else.

Nora noticed because the progress bar stuttered. Not stopped, just hesitated, like a person walking into a room and forgetting why. The terminal had been scrolling for so long that she was reading it the way one reads a highway at night—aware of motion, not content. Then one line pulsed amber at the bottom.

> ANOMALY: entry_7741.flag — encoding mismatch (0.0002%)

She leaned in. The number was too small. Cinder’s thresholds had been tuned for ordinary garbage: corrupted bytes, half-written headers, the digital equivalent of coffee stains. A point-zero-zero-zero-two percent mismatch should have been noise. Instead Cinder had paused the queue.

“Don’t be dramatic,” Nora muttered, and opened the entry.

The log viewer filled with black. Then the characters arrived.

They were not letters. They were not emoji, not mojibake, not the boxed question marks of a font that had lost its map. They were strokes—vertical, angled, hooked—standing in a row like iron pins driven into the screen. Some had branches. Some had eyes. The parser had rendered them in a font Nora had never installed, and the longer she looked, the more certain she became that they were looking back with the flat patience of something carved rather than written.

Runic, she thought. The word arrived without invitation. She was not a linguist. She had taken one Norse mythology elective in college because it satisfied a humanities requirement and because the professor had a soothing voice. But she knew runes when she saw them. These were close enough to the old alphabets to be recognizable, and far enough to be wrong. The angles were too sharp. The spacing was too even. And beneath each line, in the same malformed file, was a plain-text header that did not belong to any logging schema she knew.

> [REDACTED SEGMENT] — ritual_inputaccepted — source=user_survey_archive — yield_pending

Nora’s first instinct was to laugh. Someone in platform engineering had a sense of humor and too much access. Ritual. Yield. It was the sort of joke that got embedded in test fixtures and forgotten for years, then surfaced during an audit to terrify whoever was unlucky enough to find it.

Her second instinct was to copy it.

She did not decide to. Her fingers moved before the thought finished, highlighting the block, dragging it into a local scratch file named, with tremendous originality, notes.txt. The copy command returned. The terminal blinked.

Then the entry began to delete itself.

It was not a crash. A crash would have been honest. The line with the runes thinned, character by character, as if someone were erasing it from the other side of the glass. The plain-text header went first. The amber highlight dimmed to gray. Cinder’s progress bar resumed with a jerk, and the parser moved on to the next entry as though nothing had happened.

Nora sat very still.

The cursor blinked in her scratch file. The copied block sat there, unchanged, six lines of impossible glyphs and one line of ordinary ASCII.

> restricted_service=svc-sub-basement-04

She read it three times. The sub-basement designation was not in the building directory she had been given during orientation. It was not in the service catalog. It was not in the access matrix she had spent a week memorizing because her onboarding buddy had said, only half joking, that Reddit’s internal permissions were a haunted house and the trick was to know which doors not to open.

But the string was real. She queried the internal registry. The response came back in less than a second.

> SERVICE: svc-sub-basement-04
> STATUS: restricted
> OWNER: [not disclosed]
> ACCESS: denied (insufficient clearance)

Nora’s mouth had gone dry. Around her, the office breathed. A printer woke up somewhere and shuffled a page. The security badge reader by the elevators chirped as someone left for the night. All of it felt very far away, as if the floor had quietly detached from the rest of the building and was floating.

She should report it. That was the correct answer. She should screenshot the anomaly, flag it in the audit ticket, and let someone with a salary and a title decide what to do about a deprecated log entry that wrote in dead alphabets and referenced a room that did not exist. The instructions were clear. The audit was routine. She was a junior engineer, six months out of school, still learning where the good coffee lived.

Instead she opened the copied block again.

The runes had not changed. But the longer she stared, the more she became aware of a pattern beneath them—not meaning exactly, not translation, but rhythm. The lines were arranged like a chant. The repeated strokes at the end of each row looked like a closing, a seal, a held breath released in the same place every time. The plain-text header had called it ritual_input. She thought of the millions of user surveys Cinder had parsed that day, the little confessions and jokes and complaints of strangers, all of them reduced to rows and columns.

The cursor blinked.

Nora looked toward the dark glass of the window. Her reflection looked back, wan and tired, and behind it the city gleamed in bands of gold and white.

She copied the entry a second time, into an encrypted note, and then a third, into an email draft she did not send. Her heart was doing something complicated in her chest. Not fear yet. Not quite. It was the feeling of standing on a familiar street and noticing, for the first time, a door where no door had been.

The audit log had resumed. The progress bar climbed toward completion. Somewhere in the building, below the lobby, below the parking levels, below the neat labeled floors where people made posts and policies and profits, a service named svc-sub-basement-04 was waiting.

Nora closed the terminal, but she did not log off.

On her screen, in the scratch file, the runic entry remained—small, sharp, and patient.

She called it Cinder because it burned through old records and left only the ash of compliance.
Cinder had processed 4.8 million entries since morning.
It had found three malformed timestamps, one duplicated request ID, and a service account with a password so old it was practically archaeological.
All of it had gone into a tidy report with green checkmarks and a paragraph her manager would not read.
At 8:47 p.m., Cinder found something else.
Nora noticed because the progress bar stuttered.
Not stopped, just hesitated, like a person walking into a room and forgetting why.
The terminal had been scrolling for so long that she was reading it the way one reads a highway at night—aware of motion, not content.
Then one line pulsed amber at the bottom.
> ANOMALY: entry_7741.flag — encoding mismatch (0.0002%)
She leaned in.
The number was too small.
Cinder’s thresholds had been tuned for ordinary garbage: corrupted bytes, half-written headers, the digital equivalent of coffee stains.
A point-zero-zero-zero-two percent mismatch should have been noise.
Instead Cinder had paused the queue.
“Don’t be dramatic,” Nora muttered, and opened the entry.
The log viewer filled with black.
Then the characters arrived.
They were not letters.
They were not emoji, not mojibake, not the boxed question marks of a font that had lost its map.
They were strokes—vertical, angled, hooked—standing in a row like iron pins driven into the screen.
Some had branches.
Some had eyes.

The parser had rendered them in a font Nora had never installed, and the longer she looked, the more certain she became that they were looking back with the flat patience of something carved rather than written.
Runic, she thought.
The word arrived without invitation.
She was not a linguist.
She had taken one Norse mythology elective in college because it satisfied a humanities requirement and because the professor had a soothing voice.
But she knew runes when she saw them.
These were close enough to the old alphabets to be recognizable, and far enough to be wrong.
The angles were too sharp.
The spacing was too even.
And beneath each line, in the same malformed file, was a plain-text header that did not belong to any logging schema she knew.
> [REDACTED SEGMENT] — ritual_inputaccepted — source=user_survey_archive — yield_pending
Nora’s first instinct was to laugh.
Someone in platform engineering had a sense of humor and too much access.
Ritual.
Yield.
It was the sort of joke that got embedded in test fixtures and forgotten for years, then surfaced during an audit to terrify whoever was unlucky enough to find it.
Her second instinct was to copy it.
She did not decide to.
Her fingers moved before the thought finished, highlighting the block, dragging it into a local scratch file named, with tremendous originality, notes.txt.
The copy command returned.
The terminal blinked.
Then the entry began to delete itself.
It was not a crash.
A crash would have been honest.
The line with the runes thinned, character by character, as if someone were erasing it from the other side of the glass.
The plain-text header went first.
The amber highlight dimmed to gray.
Cinder’s progress bar resumed with a jerk, and the parser moved on to the next entry as though nothing had happened.
Nora sat very still.
The cursor blinked in her scratch file.
The copied block sat there, unchanged, six lines of impossible glyphs and one line of ordinary ASCII.
> restricted_service=svc-sub-basement-04
She read it three times.
The sub-basement designation was not in the building directory she had been given during orientation.
It was not in the service catalog.

It was not in the access matrix she had spent a week memorizing because her onboarding buddy had said, only half joking, that Reddit’s internal permissions were a haunted house and the trick was to know which doors not to open.
But the string was real.
She queried the internal registry.
The response came back in less than a second.
> SERVICE: svc-sub-basement-04
> STATUS: restricted
> OWNER: [not disclosed]
> ACCESS: denied (insufficient clearance)
Nora’s mouth had gone dry.
Around her, the office breathed.
A printer woke up somewhere and shuffled a page.
The security badge reader by the elevators chirped as someone left for the night.
All of it felt very far away, as if the floor had quietly detached from the rest of the building and was floating.
She should report it.
That was the correct answer.

She should screenshot the anomaly, flag it in the audit ticket, and let someone with a salary and a title decide what to do about a deprecated log entry that wrote in dead alphabets and referenced a room that did not exist.
The instructions were clear.
The audit was routine.
She was a junior engineer, six months out of school, still learning where the good coffee lived.
Instead she opened the copied block again.
The runes had not changed.
But the longer she stared, the more she became aware of a pattern beneath them—not meaning exactly, not translation, but rhythm.
The lines were arranged like a chant.
The repeated strokes at the end of each row looked like a closing, a seal, a held breath released in the same place every time.
The plain-text header had called it ritual_input.
She thought of the millions of user surveys Cinder had parsed that day, the little confessions and jokes and complaints of strangers, all of them reduced to rows and columns.
The cursor blinked.
Nora looked toward the dark glass of the window.
Her reflection looked back, wan and tired, and behind it the city gleamed in bands of gold and white.
She copied the entry a second time, into an encrypted note, and then a third, into an email draft she did not send.
Her heart was doing something complicated in her chest.
Not fear yet.
Not quite.
It was the feeling of standing on a familiar street and noticing, for the first time, a door where no door had been.
The audit log had resumed.
The progress bar climbed toward completion.
Somewhere in the building, below the lobby, below the parking levels, below the neat labeled floors where people made posts and policies and profits, a service named svc-sub-basement-04 was waiting.
Nora closed the terminal, but she did not log off.
On her screen, in the scratch file, the runic entry remained—small, sharp, and patient.

text:
The scratch file was still open when Nora came back the next morning, though she had closed her laptop twice and slept badly between the two closures. She had dreamed of spreadsheets with teeth. In the dream she had scrolled to the bottom of one and found her own name in a cell, formatted in bold.

She arrived at 7:12 a.m., before the floor's lights had finished waking up. The cleaning crew's cart sat abandoned by the kitchenette, smelling of lemon and bleach. She made coffee she did not drink and opened a terminal before she took off her coat.

There was a correct way to do this. Nora wrote the correct way on a sticky note and stuck it to her monitor, because she had learned in her first month that her judgment was better when it had a witness.

> 1. Scope the query to read-only.
> 2. Document every step in the ticket.
> 3. Escalate before you touch anything.

She read the note. Then she ran a read-only query, because the first two steps were compatible with curiosity.

The service registry was a sprawling, badly groomed thing, a city of accounts built by accretion. For every clean, documented service there were three older ones with names like `svc-temp-jenkins` and `billing_worker_OLD_DONOTUSE`, and Nora had spent enough of her audit learning its alleys to know where the bodies were buried. `svc-sub-basement-04` was not buried. It was simply absent from every namespace that answered to her credentials, which was not the same thing.

She started with the string itself and worked outward.

The first hit came from an internal DNS snapshot—three years old, retained for compliance, probably nobody's problem anymore. The snapshot contained a zone file for a subdomain that no longer resolved but had once existed:

> goldward.corp.reddit.internal

She typed it into a search box and got nothing, which was itself a kind of result. Internal search indexed everything, including things it shouldn't. Nothing meant the term had been scrubbed from the index, or scoped out of it, or both.

But the DNS snapshot had more. It had a comment field, and the comment field had a line in it, and the line was written by hand—an actual person, three years ago, leaving a note for whoever came after.

> migr. to GOLDWARD cluster — do not decom. ask R.M.

Nora looked at the initials for a long moment. Then she opened the org chart.

Reddit’s leadership page was public and polished. Below it, the internal directory was less polished and vastly more informative: a tree with photos and titles and, if you knew where to look, a small gray field labeled *access groups*. She ran GOLDWARD against it. Nothing. She ran `svc-sub-basement` against it. Nothing. She ran the pattern she had been building in her head for an hour—`gold.*ward`, `sub.*base`, `ritual`—and got a hit that turned out to be a marketing analytics tool called Goldward, which cost her twenty minutes and a small, humiliating meeting invitation. The real fragment came from an old incident ticket, closed and archived, where someone had pasted a Terraform module and asked why it was still billing.

> module "goldward_ops" {
>   source = "internal/terraform/modules/goldward"
>   access_group = "grp_goldward_operators"
> }

Two things surfaced at once, and Nora copied both into her notes before she did anything as stupid as reading them properly.

The first was a group. `grp_goldward_operators` was a real, live access group. It had nineteen members. She could not see their names, but she could see their attributes—their titles, their departments, the shape of their seniority—because the directory's filtering was only ever designed to hide one half of the question.

Director of Finance. VP of Infrastructure. Senior Director, Trust & Safety. Principal Engineer, Data Platform. Chief of Staff. A cluster of people so senior they usually appeared in Nora's world only as the sourceless authors of documents with titles like *Principles* and *Alignment*.

The second thing was the audit trail.

Not the one she was supposed to be reading. A second one, buried in the same bucket—a log of physical badge events for a door designated only as `SE-04`, which she had to cross-reference three ways before she understood meant Service Elevator, Bank Four. The events had a regularity that felt less like scheduling than liturgy: a few hundred scans a year, out of a device that served a floor with no listed rooms.

Nora sat back. Her coffee had gone cold again. She was starting to think of her life as a series of cold coffees.

The pattern was this: every other Thursday, between 9:40 and 10:15 p.m., a small group of people badged into SE-04 and did not badge out until between 1:00 and 2:00 a.m. The group was never the same twice, but its size was eerily consistent—nine, eleven, nine, twelve. When she joined the badge log against the directory's attributes, the overlap was total. Every after-hours scan belonged to a member of `grp_goldward_operators`.

No break-ins. No anomalies. No strangers from outside with cloned credentials. Just the executive floor going downstairs in the middle of the night, in numbers, for years.

"Morning."

Nora closed the log window so fast her mouse clicked twice. Priya from platform reliability stood at the edge of the aisle with a tote bag and a look of mild concern.

"You're here early," Priya said.

"Audit," Nora said. "Deprecated services."

"The glamorous stuff." Priya kept walking. Then she stopped, half-turned, and said, in a tone that Nora would spend the rest of the day turning over, "Hey. If you find anything weird in the old logs, don't chase it too far. There's—" A small, embarrassed laugh. "There's a lot of legacy down there. It's not always worth the headache."

"Down where?"

Priya blinked. "Down in the stack. The old stack." She gestured vaguely at the floor, the building, the concept of floors beneath other floors. "Ask your manager. Or don't. Honestly, don't." And then she was gone, tote bag swinging, and her footsteps receded toward the good coffee.

Nora wrote the whole exchange down in her notes. She wrote *she knew what I was looking at,* then looked at that sentence for a while, and didn't delete it.

By noon, she had the elevator.

It was an old badge system—one of three overlapping systems, because nothing at Reddit died, things only got layered over. The SE-04 reader still spoke to a controller that still had a web console, but the console wanted a legacy maintenance credential, the kind that lived in the audit’s own credential-hygiene report. Nora used one of the flagged accounts because it was the only key she had, and because the report was due Friday. The console logged her access with the flat indifference of a system nobody had read in five years. It was not broken. It was just unremembered. Nora found it the way you find a service account with a password so old it was practically archaeological: by looking where nobody had needed to look since before she worked there.

The console gave her the door's schedule, its firmware, its tenants. And it gave her, in a comments field last edited by a user called `rmckinley`, a note that had clearly been intended for maintenance staff:

> SE-04 serves sublevels B4-B7 only. B7 door: operator badge + fob. Do not cycle controller during the Thursday block.

Nora read the phrase *the Thursday block* four times.

She closed the console. She opened it again. She took a screenshot, and then took a screenshot of the screenshot, because a part of her had already concluded that evidence had a habit of thinning out on the other side of the glass.

Then she pulled the building directory—the real one, the facilities one, not the orientation one—and searched for the room names behind B7.

The facilities directory listed B4 as records storage. B5 as mechanical. B6 as a data center, decommissioned 2019, still cooled. B7 was not listed at all, and the directory did not have a gap where B7 should have been. It simply went from B6 to the roof.

A room that was not in the building. A door that required a ritual badge. A group of nineteen senior operators who went down at ten and came up at two, once a fortnight, for years.

Nora sat in her chair in the humming fluorescence and felt the floor give a little beneath her, the way a familiar street gives when you notice the door where no door had been.

She looked at the sticky note on her monitor. *3. Escalate before you touch anything.*

She was not going to escalate. She understood this about herself now, in the flat and frightened way one understands a diagnosis. She was going to do one more read-only query, and then another, and then she was going to stand in front of that service elevator at 9:30 on a Thursday night and see who got on it.

Her calendar told her that Thursday was three days away.

She moved her mouse back to the terminal. In the notes file, beneath the runes she had copied at 8:47 p.m. last night, she typed a new line:

> B7. SE-04. Ask R.M. — no. Don't ask.

And then, because she was a junior engineer and junior engineers are trained to leave the logs tidy, she saved the file and cleared her clipboard, and did not look at the runes again until she got home.
